title: Assessment of Protein Bioavailability from Duckweed as an Alternative Protein Source in Humans
summary:
Proteins are essential building blocks of life and play a central role in cellular structure, metabolism, and immune function. An adequate protein intake is crucial for growth, regeneration, and the maintenance of vital physiological functions. In particular, proteins are indispensable for muscle development and maintenance, enzymatic processes, and immune responses. Therefore, alternative protein sources, including plant-based, microbial, and cell-cultured proteins, are gaining increasing importance (Aiking, 2011).

Duckweed (genus Lemna) is a fast-growing aquatic plant that can be cultivated in open ponds, simple greenhouses, or vertical multi-layer cultivation systems without requiring agricultural land (Goopy & Murray, 2003; Hassan & Edwards, 1992). Under optimal conditions regarding temperature, light, nutrient availability, and regular harvesting, duckweed can achieve a high protein content of 35–43% (Appenroth et al., 2017; Goopy & Murray, 2003; Leng et al., 1995). In addition, it is rich in minerals, vitamins, carotenoids, and certain flavonoids and exhibits a favorable fatty acid composition (Appenroth et al., 2017; Edelman & Colt, 2016; Mwale & Gwaze, 2013). Particularly noteworthy is its favorable essential amino acid (EAA) profile, which is closer to that of animal-derived protein sources than that of most other plant-based proteins currently used in food products (Iqbal, 1999; Leng et al., 1995; Maag et al., 2025).

Various processing methods have been investigated to improve the digestibility and bioavailability of nutrients contained in duckweed. Among these, ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAAE) has shown promising results. The application of ultrasound disrupts plant cell structures, facilitating the release of intracellular compounds and increasing both protein yield and extraction efficiency (Maag et al., 2025; Takács et al., 2025). In addition to enhancing overall extraction efficiency, UAAE particularly promotes the recovery of hydrophobic amino acids and specific dietary fibers that contribute to emulsion stability. The resulting protein isolate contains approximately 65% protein and exhibits an amino acid profile that meets the recommendations of the WHO/FAO/UNU for preschool children. Despite these advantages, ultrasound-assisted technologies are currently rarely applied in the direct production of duckweed-based foods, representing an emerging innovation potential in the field of functional foods and alternative proteins.

interventions.name: Administration of a test meal providing 20 g of duckweed protein, with subsequent blood sampling at predefined time points (baseline, 15 min, 30 min, 45 min, 1 h, 1.5 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, and 24 h) to assess postprandial amino acid availability.

Administration of a test meal providing 20 g of ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAAE)-treated duckweed protein, followed by blood sampling at predefined time points (0 min, 15 min, 30 min, 45 min, 1 h, 1.5 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, and 24 h) to evaluate postprandial amino acid availability.

Administration of 20 g of egg protein, followed by blood sampling at predefined time points (0, 15, 30, and 45 minutes, and 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 6, and 24 hours) to assess postprandial amino acid availability.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Age 18–40 years
- Body mass index (BMI) ≥ 18,5 kg/m²
- Male and female participants
- Written informed consent provided prior to study participation
Exclusion criteria:
- Lack of written informed consent
- Current participation in another interventional clinical study
- Pregnancy or breastfeeding
- Smoking
- Competitive athletes (>16 hours of training per week)
- Acute or chronic infections (e.g., HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, tuberculosis)
- Untreated hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism
- Implanted cardiac pacemaker
- Cancer within the last 6 months or completion of radiochemotherapy within the last 3 years
- Long-term gastrointestinal disorders (e.g., inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease)
- Known history of diabetes mellitus requiring current medication at the time of screening
- Acute gastrointestinal disorders (e.g., diarrhea) or bleeding disorders
- Planned surgery during the intervention period
- Known allergies or intolerances to the tested food products
- Regular use of protein supplements
